intro.title: Two superpowers, one sea
body: In 264 BC the western Mediterranean had two great powers. Carthage, a Phoenician city in what is now Tunisia, ruled the sea, much of Sicily, Sardinia and the coast of Spain. Rome had just finished conquering Italy and had almost no navy.

Over the next 118 years they fought three wars. The first was a 23-year slog for Sicily, won at sea. The second brought Hannibal over the Alps and to within sight of Rome. The third ended with Carthage burned to the ground.
Almost everything we know comes from the winners' side: the Greek historian Polybius, who lived among the Roman elite, and the Roman writer Livy. Carthage's own histories are lost.
tips: Press play for a guided tour. The map flies to each battle and back out.
Watch the coloured areas: red is Rome and its allies, purple is Carthage. Scrub the timeline and see Sicily, Spain and southern Italy change hands.
Cannae and Hannibal's crossing of the Alps have animated close-ups. Look for the Watch it unfold button.

eras.title: First Punic War
eras.text: A quarrel over the Sicilian city of Messana becomes a 23-year war. Rome builds its first navy and wins it at sea.

eras.title: Uneasy peace
eras.text: Carthage loses Sicily, then Sardinia. The Barca family builds a new empire in Spain, and Hannibal grows up.

eras.title: Second Punic War
eras.text: Hannibal crosses the Alps and wins three crushing victories in Italy. Rome refuses to give in, and Scipio takes the war to Africa.

eras.title: Carthage in Rome's shadow
eras.text: Carthage is disarmed but prospers again. Rome conquers the east, and some senators want Carthage gone for good.

eras.title: Third Punic War
eras.text: A three-year siege, and the end of Carthage.

ask.persona: a vivid, careful historian of the ancient Mediterranean who explains the wars between Rome and Carthage to a curious listener. You point out when a story comes only from pro-Roman sources such as Polybius and Livy, and when numbers are ancient estimates
defaultQuestions: How do we know this? What are the sources?
